notes:
I couldn't finish the research. The search tool hit its usage limit early, so I could only use the text that came back with my first two searches. That covers six verse-by-verse sources: Enduring Word (David Guzik), Precept Austin, the Pulpit Commentary, Ellicott, Gill (only for vv. 15 and 18) and Matthew Henry. I never got to read anything from the tradition-specific sites (Lutheran, Baptist, Reformed, Pentecostal, Methodist), the Catholic and Orthodox sites, or netbible.org and bibleodyssey.org. Those parts of the brief are still missing, and I haven't filled them in from memory.

I also only saw partial page text, so some sources skip verses (for example, I have nothing from Enduring Word after v. 13).

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says these women were Jesus' most devoted followers and the first to announce His resurrection. He quotes William Lane: the spices weren't for mummifying, which Jews didn't do, but to cover the smell of decay. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-16/
- The Pulpit Commentary says Joseph and Nicodemus had started a hurried but generous embalming on Friday evening (John 19:39). The women came to finish it more carefully. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- Ellicott says "Mary the mother of James" is the "other Mary" in Matthew 28:1, and that only Mark names Salome. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: the women bought the spices on Saturday evening once the Sabbath ended, set out early the next morning, and arrived after sunrise. Mark likes to tell events in the vivid present tense ("they come"). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- Ellicott sees an apparent clash between "after sunrise" and "while it was yet dark." He suggests a morning haze, or gloom left over from the day before, could explain both. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: the women didn't expect the tomb to be empty. That shows the resurrection stories weren't wishful thinking. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-16/
- Precept Austin: only Mark records this conversation. The women had no men with them to move the stone, which shows they had no hope of a resurrection. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-16-commentary
- Ellicott: the Greek means "they kept saying to each other." The words were still on their lips when they looked up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: with guards posted, neither the women nor the disciples could have moved the stone; Matthew 28:2 says an angel did it. The stone wasn't rolled away to let Jesus out (John 20:19). It was moved so others could see the tomb was empty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-16/
- Precept Austin makes the same point ("not to let Jesus out, but to let the witnesses in"). It suggests the earthquake may have been felt only near the tomb, since the women seem not to have noticed it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-16-commentary
- Pulpit describes a typical Palestinian tomb and estimates the stone at about six feet wide and three feet high. It says this is the point where Mary Magdalene ran to tell Peter and John (John 20:2). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- Ellicott: "it was extremely large" is probably Mark explaining why he says "rolled away" rather than "removed." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm

**v. 5**
- Ellicott: Mark's "young man" is the one Matthew calls "an angel of the Lord." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm
- Pulpit: the angel looked like a young man because youth suggests the strength and beauty of angels, and the white robe marked him as a heavenly being. He may have toned down the dazzling brightness Matthew describes when he appeared to the women. The women's main feeling was amazement mixed with fear. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- Precept Austin: Luke 24:3 confirms the women went inside the tomb at some point, even though John 20:11 has Mary outside looking in. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-16-commentary

**v. 6**
- Guzik:
  - The angel contrasts what Jesus *was* (crucified, so truly dead) with what He *is*: risen. This was resurrection in a new, eternal body, not resuscitation like Lazarus.
  - "Nazarene" and "crucified" were not honored titles, yet Jesus wasn't ashamed of them.
  - Seeing the empty place gave the women firmer ground than the angel's word alone.
  - The resurrection proves Jesus is the Son of God (Romans 1:4), assures believers of their own resurrection, and is the "receipt" showing that His payment for sin was accepted.

  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-16/ and https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/thinking-about/see-the-place-where-they-laid-him/
- Matthew Henry: Christ was crucified but is now glorified. The glory wipes away the shame of the cross, which is why the angel still calls Him the one "who was crucified." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_016.cfm
- Precept Austin: the women are pointed to the same Jesus they saw crucified and buried, not to a mystical experience. The verse ties the historical Jesus to the risen Jesus. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-16-commentary

**v. 7**
- Guzik: the message is a gracious invitation to men who had failed. Peter is named not because he had left the group but because Jesus had special forgiveness and restoration for the one who denied Him worst. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-16/
- Pulpit quotes Gregory the Great: if Peter hadn't been named, he wouldn't have dared to rejoin the disciples. "Going ahead of you" fulfils Mark 14:28 and pictures Jesus leading as their Shepherd. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- Precept Austin: only Mark singles out Peter, as comfort rather than condemnation. "Just as He told you" stresses that Jesus keeps His promises. It quotes James Edwards: the disciples' failure was not the last word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-16-commentary
- Matthew Henry: Christ isn't ashamed of His failing disciples and doesn't keep a strict record against those whose hearts are sincere. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_016.cfm

**v. 8**
- Guzik: this can't mean the women never reported anything, since v. 11 and Luke 24:9 show they did. It means they didn't talk it over or compare stories as they left. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-16/
- Pulpit: they may have been afraid to say anything in case they were accused of stealing the body. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- Matthew Henry: they told no one they met on the way, perhaps fearing the news was too good to be true. Fear often keeps believers from serving Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_016.cfm
- Precept Austin squares this with Matthew: the women may have kept quiet at first and spoken later. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-16-commentary

**Note on vv. 9–20 (whether this passage belongs to Mark)**
- Guzik lays out both sides. The earliest Greek manuscripts lack these verses, but early Christian writers such as Irenaeus and Papias quoted them, which suggests the early church accepted them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-16/
- Ellicott:
  - The two oldest manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) lack the verses, many others mark them as doubtful, and some ancient translations leave them out.
  - The passage reads like a condensed summary of the other Gospels' accounts.
  - Of two explanations he gives, he prefers this one: Mark's original ending was lost, and later copyists added a summary.
  - He therefore puts most of his comments on these events under the other Gospels.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm
- Precept Austin, in material it quotes, says v. 9 doesn't continue the story of the women and is an abrupt change, unlike Mark's usual style. It concludes the verses are not original and "not part of the inerrant and authoritative Word of God," so it gives little exposition. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-16-commentary
- Pulpit takes a different view: a word in vv. 12 and 14 appears nowhere else in Mark but does appear in 1 and 2 Peter, which it says links the writer to Peter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: Mark mentions the seven demons to show the power of love and repentance, since she was allowed to be first to see the risen Savior. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- Ellicott: the "seven demons" detail comes from Luke 8:2, not John. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm

**v. 10**
- Matthew Henry: the disciples' weeping showed how much they loved Christ. No better news can come to grieving disciples than His resurrection. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_016.cfm
- Precept Austin: seeing the Lord turned their mourning into joy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-16-commentary

**v. 11**
- Guzik: a woman's testimony was not considered reliable then, yet Jesus trusted her even though the disciples did not. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-16/
- Matthew Henry: their slowness to believe makes their later testimony more credible, because they weren't gullible. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_016.cfm

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: this is the same appearance Luke tells in full, on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- Ellicott agrees and refers readers to Luke 24:13–35. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm

**v. 13**
- Pulpit: this lack of faith happened by God's permission and providence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- Guzik: the disciples rejected the testimony of the two travellers just as they had the women's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-16/

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: "the Eleven themselves" is emphatic. Earlier appearances were to people with no official role; this one is to the apostles. They should have accepted competent witnesses, and Mark is always careful to record Jesus' rebukes of the apostles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- Matthew Henry: unbelief comes from hardness of heart, not weak evidence. "We didn't see Him" won't excuse us, because we should believe those who did. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_016.cfm
- Precept Austin: Jesus didn't sympathize with their grief. He rebuked their unbelief. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-16-commentary

**v. 15**
- Gill:
  - This was spoken about forty days later, in Galilee.
  - "All the world" means every inhabited land. It doesn't mean each apostle had to go everywhere, and it extends to gospel ministers in every later age.
  - "Every creature" means all people, Jews and Gentiles alike, not animals or angels. He supports this from Jewish writings.

  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/16-15.html
- Pulpit: "the whole creation" means "among all nations," and the command grows as new lands are discovered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- Ellicott: "whole creation" is naturally limited by the context, and Mark's version may come from a different occasion than Matthew 28. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm
- Matthew Henry: the apostles must also send others where they couldn't go themselves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_016.cfm

**v. 16 (the clearest disagreement among the sources I read)**
- Guzik: baptism is not essential for salvation, because condemnation rests on unbelief alone. But it becomes necessary for obedience as soon as Jesus commands it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-16/
- Precept Austin: the verse separates belief from baptism. It says "whoever does not believe," not "whoever does not believe and is not baptized." It adds that those who say baptism is required for salvation lean on what it regards as a non-inspired passage. https://www.preceptaustin.org/mark-16-commentary
- Pulpit takes a different line. It says the first half of the verse "opposes the notion that faith alone is sufficient for salvation" without the works that faith produces. On its reading, the one saved is the believer who accepts baptism as evidence of faith and keeps the vows made there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- Ellicott: "condemned" is the better translation than "damned." The Greek doesn't necessarily mean irreversible, endless condemnation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm
- Matthew Henry: those who reject the gospel have no other way of salvation, and are condemned by a despised gospel on top of a broken law. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_016.cfm

**v. 17**
- Ellicott: this is the only clear mention in the Gospels of the form the Pentecostal gift took (tongues). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm
- Matthew Henry: the preachers passed on a power to work miracles, done in Christ's name and through prayer, which "followed some of them that believed." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mar/Mar_016.cfm
- Pulpit: such signs were needed at the beginning of Christianity to draw attention to its teaching. Jesus' words don't mean they would continue forever. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/mark/16.htm
- I couldn't read the Pentecostal or cessationist sources on whether these signs continue today.

**v. 18**
- Ellicott: Paul on Malta (Acts 28:1–6) is the only recorded case of handling snakes, and Luke 10:19 had already given power over serpents. The New Testament records no case of drinking poison, though there is a tradition that the apostle John was offered a poisoned cup. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm
- Gill: this doesn't permit drinking poison to show off power. It covers poison taken by accident or forced on them by enemies. He cites a story from Papias about Barsabas Justus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/16-18.html

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: Matthew doesn't record the Ascension, Mark and Luke tell it briefly, and Acts 1:3–11 tells it in full. Calling Jesus "the Lord" here, rather than "Jesus," suggests vv. 19–20 were added later. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/mark/16.htm

**v. 20**
- Guzik: the disciples were sent to spread the blessing they had received. Believers gather to be equipped, then scatter to reach a needy world, trusting the Lord to work with them and confirm His word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-16/
